Because many are lipophilic, they would otherwise accumulate in tissues and resist renal elimination.
These exogenous chemical compounds foreign to normal human biochemistry undergo biotransformation to become more water-soluble for excretion.

terms.sub: Phase I Reactions and Cytochrome P450
clues: It explains why a harmless-looking chemical can cause liver necrosis, mutagenicity, or cancer.
Examples include conversion of aflatoxin B1 to an epoxide or acetaminophen to a reactive quinone imine.
This process occurs when Phase I metabolism converts a relatively inert xenobiotic into a more toxic or electrophilic metabolite.
It is a tripeptide composed of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine whose sulfhydryl group neutralizes electrophiles and peroxides.
Depletion of its hepatic stores during acetaminophen overdose permits unopposed hepatocyte injury.
Abbreviated GSH, it is conjugated to electrophilic xenobiotics by S-transferases and serves as a major cellular antioxidant.
It forms after sequential removal of glutamate and glycine from a glutathione conjugate followed by N-acetylation.
It is a classic urinary biomarker of exposure to electrophilic xenobiotics and alkylating agents.
This N-acetylated cysteine derivative represents the final excreted product of a detoxification pathway.
It is formed primarily by hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes (including CYP2E1) during acetaminophen metabolism.
N-acetylcysteine prevents liver injury by replenishing the thiol stores that normally detoxify it.
This reactive electrophilic quinone imine causes centrilobular hepatic necrosis when acetaminophen overdose overwhelms glutathione conjugation.
It is preferred over ethanol in clinical practice because it avoids central nervous system intoxication and hypoglycemia.
By blocking conversion of parent alcohols into formic acid or glycolic/oxalic acid, it prevents severe metabolic acidosis and organ damage.
This antidote competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase to treat methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning.
It uses histidine-requiring mutant strains of Salmonella typhimurium to test for reverse mutations.
Rat liver S9 homogenate is often added to detect procarcinogens that require metabolic activation.
This widely used bacterial assay screens chemicals for mutagenic potential.
Roughly one-third of its amino acid residues are cysteines whose thiol groups bind metal ions tightly.
Exposure to zinc, copper, or cadmium induces its synthesis.
This small metal-binding protein helps buffer intracellular heavy metal toxicity and regulate essential trace metals.
